title: Complex Integration
body:
You cannot integrate from $a$ to $b$ in the plane without saying **which way you went**, so a complex
integral is taken along a curve:

$$
\int_\gamma f(z)\,dz = \int_a^b f(\gamma(t))\,\gamma'(t)\,dt
$$

Parameterise the contour, substitute, and it collapses to an ordinary real integral of a complex
integrand. This is structurally the [[Line Integral]] from [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]], with the same
[[Parameterization]] step, and the analogies keep going: Cauchy's theorem below plays the role
[[Green's Theorem]] plays there, which is not a coincidence since one can be derived from the other.

## Cauchy's theorem and formula

**If $f$ is analytic everywhere inside and on a closed contour $\gamma$, then
$\oint_\gamma f(z)\,dz = 0$.** The integral of a well-behaved function around any closed loop
vanishes, so between two points the path does not matter, only the endpoints. That is the same
statement a [[Conservative Vector Field]] makes in vector calculus.

The consequence is that **all the value of a contour integral lives at the singularities**, the
points where $f$ fails to be analytic. Cauchy's integral formula pins it down:

$$
f(z_0) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_\gamma \frac{f(z)}{z - z_0}\,dz
$$

The values of an analytic function on a closed curve determine its value at every point inside.
Nothing in real analysis behaves like that, and it is the reason analytic functions are so rigid.

## The one integral to remember

$$
\oint_{|z| = r} \frac{dz}{z} = 2\pi i
$$

Everything else is bookkeeping around this. Parameterise the circle as $z = re^{i\theta}$, so
$dz = ire^{i\theta}d\theta$, and the integrand becomes $i\,d\theta$ integrated from 0 to $2\pi$. The
$e^{i\theta}$ cancels, the radius does not appear, and **every other power $z^n$ integrates to zero**
around the loop because it comes back to where it started. Only the $-1$ power survives, which is
precisely why the [[Residue Theorem]] cares about that one coefficient and nothing else.

See [[Complex Exponential]] for the parameterisation and [[Complex Convergence]] for where the
singularities are.
